title: Given a set of words and a typed prefix, return all words that start with that prefix, optionally limited to the top few. Explain how the Trie pattern provides autocomplete, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Autocomplete Suggestions (Return Words Matching a Typed Prefix)
keyPoints: Walk from the trie root to the prefix node, then collect every complete word in the subtree below it.
If any character in the prefix has no matching child, no word starts with that prefix and the result is empty.
Depth-first search from the prefix node gathers all suggestions, building up suffixes as it descends.
Storing children in sorted order yields alphabetical suggestions naturally.
An early return once enough suggestions are gathered enforces a top-few limit efficiently.
Reaching the prefix node costs O(prefix length); gathering costs O(matched subtree size).

s1_definition.oneliner: Walk to the prefix node in the trie, then collect every complete word in the subtree below it using depth-first search.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Prefix walk** – traverse the trie from the root following the typed prefix characters to reach the prefix node.
- **No match** – if any character has no matching child, no word starts with the prefix; return empty.
- **Subtree collection** – run DFS from the prefix node, building suffixes and recording complete words (nodes marked as word ends).
- **Sorted order** – if children are stored in a TreeMap or sorted array, suggestions come out alphabetically.
- **Limit enforcement** – an early return once the result reaches the desired count avoids scanning the entire subtree.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India offers a search box where a teller types the start of a payee name and the system instantly suggests all registered payees beginning with those letters. A trie walks straight to the typed prefix and collects every name underneath it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Autocomplete Two-Phase Flow
============================

Trie (words: RAJESH, RAJIV, PRIYA)

  (root)
  ├── P
  │   └── R
  │       └── I
  │           └── Y
  │               └── A [WORD]
  └── R
      └── A
          └── J  ← prefix node for "RAJ"
              ├── E
              │   └── S
              │       └── H [WORD]
              └── I
                  └── V [WORD]


Phase 1: Walk to prefix node
─────────────────────────────
  R → A → J (arrived at prefix node)

Phase 2: DFS from prefix node
─────────────────────────────
  Current: "RAJ"
  ├── E: "RAJE"
  │   └── S: "RAJES"
  │       └── H: "RAJESH" [WORD] → collect!
  └── I: "RAJI"
      └── V: "RAJIV" [WORD] → collect!

Result: ["RAJESH", "RAJIV"]


Limit Enforcement
==================

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  results.size() >= limit?    │
  │  Yes → return immediately    │
  │  No → continue DFS           │
  └──────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Autocomplete Suggestions is a prefix-collection application of the Trie data structure, and the algorithm has two clean phases. First, walk from the trie root to the prefix node by following each character. If any character has no matching child, no word starts with that prefix and the result is empty. Second, run DFS from the prefix node, building up suffixes as you descend and recording complete words at nodes marked as word ends.

Using a TreeMap for children means the DFS visits them in sorted order, producing alphabetical suggestions naturally. An early return once the result reaches the desired limit avoids scanning the entire subtree, which is important for hot prefixes with thousands of matches.

At the National Bank of India, a teller types the first few letters of a registered payee name and expects instant suggestions. The trie is warmed from the database at startup and serves keystrokes from memory. Hot prefixes are cached in Redis for even faster response, and frequency-based ranking ensures the most relevant payees appear first.

The key performance insight is that reaching the prefix node costs only O(prefix length), and gathering suggestions costs O(matched subtree size). With a limit, the cost is bounded by the limit times the average word length, making this practical even for very large dictionaries.

Remember one sentence: walk to the prefix node in the trie, then DFS the subtree below it to collect every matching word.
